hero.title: Skimming Keyword Extraction in Précis Writing
hero.description: Skimming and keyword extraction form the bedrock of precise précis writing for the Allahabad High Court RO/ARO and UPPSC examinations. Mastery of this skill enables candidates to distill lengthy judicial, administrative, or socio-economic passages into exactly one-third of their original length while preserving the central core and logical flow without personal interpolations.

items.question: What is the mandatory target length percentage for a standard AHC RO/ARO précis?
items.answer: Exactly one-third (33%) of the original word count of the source passage.

items.question: Should direct quotations from the original passage be retained in the précis?
items.answer: No. Direct quotes must be converted into indirect speech or summarized in your own words.

items.question: What tense and person are mandatory for drafting a professional précis?
items.answer: Third-person perspective ('He', 'She', 'It', 'The author', 'The court') and appropriate past/present tense mirroring the source text.

items.question: Is it permissible to add external facts or personal critique if it improves the argument?
items.answer: Strictly prohibited. The précis must rely exclusively on the facts provided in the passage without any outside interpolation.

traps.title: Common Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Retaining Figures of Speech & Examples: Candidates often waste precious word count by retaining detailed narrative examples and metaphors from the original text. Always abstract the underlying principle instead of keeping the story.

Trap 2: Writing in First or Second Person: Using phrases like 'We understand from the passage...' or 'You can see that...' will invite severe negative marks. Always maintain strict third-person objective narrative stance.
Trap 3: Omitting the Title: Failing to provide a precise title due to time constraints leads to direct loss of marks, as title formulation is a mandatory component of official evaluation rubrics.

Mastery of this skill enables candidates to distill lengthy judicial, administrative, or socio-economic passages into exactly one-third of their original length while preserving the central core and logical flow without personal interpolations.

sections.title: Techniques of Skimming and Central Theme Identification
sections.content:
Skimming is a rapid reading strategy meant to give a bird’s-eye view of the text before detailed analysis.

  • Topic Sentence Extraction: Focus primarily on the first and last sentences of paragraphs where authors typically state and summarize their primary arguments.
  • Ignoring Elaborative Details: Deliberately bypass statistical minutiae, illustrative anecdotes, rhetorical flourishes, and parenthetical digressions during skimming.
  • Identification of Core Legal/Administrative Entities: Highlight statutory bodies, constitutional articles (e.g., Article 226, 21), court judgments, and policy mandates that anchor the text.
  • Thematic Synthesis: Combine scattered sub-arguments into a unified central theme statement that dictates the trajectory of the ensuing précis.

sections.title: Proportion, Redundancy Elimination, and Objectivity
sections.content:
Maintaining exact length limits and absolute neutrality separates top-scoring candidates in high court examinations.

  • One-Third Length Rule: The final précis must strictly adhere to 33% (one-third) of the source word count. If the passage has 300 words, the précis must be around 100 words.
  • Elimination of Redundancy: Replace lengthy descriptive phrases with single compact administrative terms (e.g., substitute 'steps taken for the welfare of impoverished citizens' with 'welfare measures').
  • Ban on Personal Opinions: Never use phrases like 'In my opinion', 'I believe', or add external critiques. Reflect only the author’s exact viewpoint with complete objectivity.
  • Indirect Speech & Third Person Convention: Write exclusively in the third person ('The author states that...', 'The judgment emphasizes...') avoiding direct quotes or first/second-person pronouns.

sections.title: Title Formulation and Logical Cohesion
sections.content:
A precise title acts as the umbrella under which the entire summary operates, while logical flow maintains readability.

  • Nature of a Good Title: The title must be brief (3 to 6 words), punchy, and encapsulate the absolute essence of the passage without being overly broad or cryptic.
  • Preserving Logical Flow: Ensure smooth transitions between sentences using subtle conjunctions (therefore, consequently, however) reflecting the original author's sequence of thought.
  • Avoidance of Questions as Titles: Titles should never be framed as interrogative questions (e.g., 'Is Justice Delayed?'); instead, use declarative noun phrases ('Causes of Judicial Delay').
